papers.title: The contribution of Neanderthal ancestry to cancer risk
papers.abstract: Modern human genomes harbor DNA inherited from interbreeding with Neanderthals. Genetic variants inherited from Neanderthals associate with variation in many immune and metabolic phenotypes, two systems with direct relevance to cancer. However, the influence of Neanderthal variants on germline cancer risk has not been comprehensively evaluated. Here, we evaluated genome-wide association study (GWAS) hits for 17 cancer types for Neanderthal ancestry. Twelve cancers have multiple Neanderthal alleles significantly associated with variation in risk. Next, we fine-mapped these risk loci and identified 32 associations across seven cancers where Neanderthal variants are likely causal (>= posterior inclusion probability). Fine-mapped loci include Neanderthal alleles that both increase and decrease cancer risk. Nine of the 32 Neanderthal associations, including the high frequency BNC2 Neanderthal variants, have signatures of adaptive introgression, and several suggest evidence of both mediated and antagonistic pleiotropy. Finally, we tested for enrichment of cancer heritability in genomic regions with Neanderthal ancestry. As expected, Neanderthal variants are depleted of heritability for most cancers. However, Neanderthal variants were enriched for heritability in breast cancer GWAS in both East Asian and Europeans, and this enrichment replicated using individual-level UK Biobank data. These results suggest that Neanderthal alleles that influence germline cancer risk were largely selected against. However, introgressed Neanderthal variants implicated in many cancers persist, potentially due to adaptive pleiotropic effects. This evolutionary perspective provides new insights into the complex evolution and etiology of cancer risk among modern human populations.

papers.title: Gene-based map of cardiovascular diseases
papers.abstract: Background: Rare coding variants contribute to cardiovascular disease, but their effects across disease groups remain incompletely characterized. In particular, the influence of functionally and clinically informed variant classification and sex-specific genetic effects on gene-phenotype associations remains understudied. Methods: We analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from up to 483,311 UK Biobank participants across six genetic ancestry groups and eight cardiovascular phenotype groups. Gene-burden testing integrated state-of-the-art missense classification and predicted pathogenic germline variants. We performed combined-sex and sex-stratified analyses, followed by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We additionally adjusted for cardiometabolic traits in sensitivity analyses, estimated penetrance among qualifying-variant carriers, and assessed genetic prevalence across eight ancestry groups. Results: We identified 86 exome-wide significant gene-phenotype associations: 40 established and 46 novel. Novel associations included EHMT2 with atrial fibrillation, P2RX1 with arrhythmias, P2RY4 with complete atrioventricular block, and NOSTRIN with atherosclerotic heart disease in females. After cardiometabolic adjustment, 60 associations retained exome-wide significance and 18 additional associations emerged, including CDH11, PARVA, and ADAMDEC1 with atherosclerosis-related phenotypes. Conclusions: These findings identify novel cardiovascular gene-phenotype associations implicating purinergic signaling, endothelial nitric oxide regulation, and vascular wall biology. Variant selection shapes penetrance estimates and the interpretation of inherited susceptibility.

papers.title: "Wow, this could be massive": Donor-Conceived Families Experience with Unexpected Recontact for Risk of Inherited Cardiac Conditions
papers.abstract: Introduction: Recontacting families post-gamete donation, after a genetic diagnosis is made in the donor, can create complex challenges for healthcare providers and families. However, there is little literature that explores the family experience. This study aimed to explore the experiences of parents and donor-conceived young people navigating the recontact process and undergoing predictive genetic testing for an inherited cardiac condition. Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants' experiences in unexpectedly being recontacted and undergoing predictive genetic testing for an inherited cardiac condition. Interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. A reflexive thematic analysis was performed. Results: Thirteen participants agreed to be interviewed, nine were parents and four were donor conceived young people. Four overarching themes were identified: (1) Out of the Blue, (2) A ripple effect on the family, (3) Calm after the storm, (4) Beneath the Ripples: the psychological impact. Discussion: Interviews provided insights into fertility services recontact and the predictive genetic testing process. From the themes, we conceptualize a ripple effect model. Findings highlight how cardiac genetics and fertility services are evolving, and the critical role of genetic counselors. The recontact process affects the entire family. However, most participants adapted and moved forward from this event.

papers.title: How inherited variation shapes human disease trajectories
papers.abstract: Although inherited variation is fixed at birth, its effects on health change with age and differ between common and rare variants. Here, we introduce Mendelnoulli, a longitudinal model that combines the age-dependent effects of polygenic and monogenic variation on health records, separating how much disease each individual accumulates overall from diseases to which they are prone. Mendelnoulli further allows polygenic and monogenic components to exert different influences on latent disease trajectories. We apply the model to 348 diseases, 36 polygenic scores, and 34 monogenic conditions across three biobanks and provide an atlas of the age-dependent effects of inherited variation on common human diseases. We show that polygenic effects change significantly with age, with Mendelnoulli improving held-out one-year discrimination for all 28 diseases tested compared with a model whose polygenic effects are constant over age (median AUC 0.95 vs 0.92). For individuals with no prior diagnoses, Mendelnoulli identified 8.6 more of every 100 new cases than that model, when each flagged the 5% at highest risk. For genes with an established disease, Mendelnoulli selected that disease for 27 of 30 genes and ranked it first for 17 (7 expected by chance), and recovered known differences in timing, such as earlier breast cancer effects for BRCA1 than BRCA2 (peak 48 vs 66 years). Mendelnoulli provides a unified model of common and rare genetic influences on disease trajectories across the life course.

papers.title: The phenomic landscape of rare gain- and loss-of-function variation
papers.abstract: Current large-scale phenome-wide association studies do not distinguish between genetic variants with distinct functional consequences, despite evidence that gain-of-function (GoF) and loss-of-function (LoF) variants can produce different phenotypes. Consequently, the phenotypic consequences of variants stratified by predicted GoF and LoF effects have not been systematically characterized at scale. Here, we systematically analyzed rare predicted GoF and LoF variants in 18,214 genes across 1,244 binary and 202 quantitative traits using whole-exome sequencing and electronic health records from the Mount Sinai Million Health Discoveries Program, a phenotypically rich hospital-based biobank comprised of 50,067 participants, primarily representing African, Admixed American and European ancestries. We identified numerous established and previously unreported ancestry-specific and shared gene- and variant-level associations, many of which were supported by complementary evidence from both diagnostic phenotypes and clinical measurements. Proteomic evaluation of the previously unreported association between VNN1 LoF variants and body mass index in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis revealed reduced circulating vanin-1 levels with LoF variants, which in turn were associated with body composition and additional cardiometabolic phenotypes. Functional stratification of predicted GoF and LoF variants revealed gene-trait associations that were attenuated when these variants were combined, demonstrating that traditional aggregation of variants with different functional effects can obscure association signals. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating predicted functional consequences into association analyses and establish a comprehensive resource linking exome-wide predicted GoF and LoF variants to the human phenome across ancestry-specific and multi-ancestry analyses.

papers.title: Cancer risk and survival outcomes in germline POT1 variant carriers
papers.abstract: Background: The prevalence of germline POT1 variants, spectrum of associated tumors, cancer risk and survival outcomes are incompletely described, and clinical management guidelines vary. We evaluated POT1 variant carriers in three biobanks and a clinical cohort to address these limitations. Methods: Prevalence, cancer spectrum and risk associated with germline POT1 pathogenic/likely pathogenic and additional functionally assessed variants were evaluated in Penn Medicine Biobank (PMBB; n=51,172), Geisinger MyCode (MyCode; n=220,582), UK Biobank (UKBB; n=469,558) and a Penn Medicine clinical cohort. Results: Estimated POT1 variant prevalence ranged from 1:1,279 to 1:2,902. Compared to non-carriers, cancer diagnoses were more frequent among POT1 variant carriers in PMBB (OR 3.41, 95%CI 1.81-6.43, p=1.88x10-4), MyCode (OR 2.23, 95%CI 1.31-3.79, p=0.003), and UKBB (OR 1.40, 95%CI 1.07-1.84, p=0.015). Cancer incidence increased beginning in the mid-30s, without evidence of increased mortality. Along with previously described cancer types, lung cancer was associated with POT1 variant carriers in two biobank cohorts. Conclusion: POT1 is a cancer susceptibility gene associated with a moderate (1.5-3.5-fold) increased cancer risk. Variants are relatively frequent and predispose to a broad tumor spectrum and increased incidence starting in the mid-30s, without increasing mortality. These findings expand understanding of POT1-associated disease and provide data to inform clinical management.

papers.title: Enrichment of Rare Exonic Variants in Cognitive Superagers from Centenarian Families
papers.abstract: Although cognitive decline and dementia are common at advanced ages, a fraction of individuals reach extreme ages maintaining high levels of cognitive function. Here, we compared whole-exome sequencing data from 136 cognitive superagers, individuals whose memory performance matches normative expectations for persons ~30 years younger, to 114 average-cognition controls and the gnomAD population reference database. While standard single-variant and burden analyses did not identify exome-wide significant loci, a rare variant allele frequency analysis identified 114 significant rare coding variants enriched in cognitive superagers. We highlight ten significant missense variants in genes implicating neurovascular biology (LOX, CLEC4M, CBWD6), immune regulation (HLA-B, HLA-DRB1, ITGAX, MUC4, MUC1), and neuronal structural (CEP131 x2). Together, these findings support an extreme-phenotype strategy as a tractable discovery framework for rare coding variation and nominate a set of biologically plausible loci to reveal potential genetic mechanisms for resilience to age-related cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Genetic architecture and polygenic prediction of self-reported response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in individuals with depression: a genome-wide meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are first-line treatments for depression, but response is highly variable, and no robust genetic predictors have been identified. We conducted a genome-wide association meta-analysis of self-reported SSRI response in 62,879 individuals of European ancestry with depression (72.6% responders) across six cohorts (seven datasets), followed by gene-set, transcriptomic, proteomic, drug-target and polygenic score (PGS) analyses. SNP-based heritability was modest but significant (h2 = 3.1%, SE = 1.4%) with no genome-wide significant variants detected. Gene-set analyses implicated gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission, and a gene involved in glutamate transport (SLC17A6) showed consistent sub-threshold evidence across pathway, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. Drug-target enrichment for hypnotics, anxiolytics and general anesthetics further supported the GABAergic signal. A leave-one-out PGS from the discovery meta-analysis was associated with self-reported SSRI response in independent cohorts (meta-analysis OR = 1.05, 95% CI 1.02--1.08, p = 0.002). Higher PGS for depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), autism, addiction and schizophrenia were associated with lower odds of reported SSRI response, with ADHD, PTSD, autism and addiction remaining after adjustment for depression PGS. In contrast, educational attainment PGS was associated with better SSRI response. Self-reported SSRI response captures genetic insights relevant to antidepressant response, implicating GABAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission. Individuals with higher genetic loading for psychiatric conditions report poorer response, and higher genetic loading for educational attainment PGS a better reported response. Although larger studies are needed to identify specific variants, self-report offers a practical, patient-centered and scalable route to collect the larger samples required.

papers.title: Transdiagnostic Psychiatric Polygenic Scores Reveal Pleiotropic Effects Across Medical and Laboratory Phenome
papers.abstract: Summary Background Current psychiatric diagnoses lack biological grounding. Using transdiagnostic psychiatric dimensions derived through data-driven genetic studies with large-scale clinical health records of multiple physiological and clinical outcomes, we can gain new insights into biological similarity and differences between such dimensions, informing nosological discourse. Methods Here, we examined data from 108,182 individuals of European-like ancestry and 13,229 African-like ancestry across two healthcare biobanks. Genetic liabilities of individuals were estimated as polygenic scores for five first-order psychopathology factors (compulsive, thought, neurodevelopmental, substance use, internalizing disorders) and one second-order factor (hierarchical/p-factor). Phenome-wide and laboratory-wide association scans encompassed 1,520 medical phenotypes and 123 laboratory metrics, meta-analyzed across sites. People with lived experience were involved in the design, preparation, interpretation and reporting of this work. Outcomes We observed robust associations with up to 143 conditions (14 disease categories) for first-order factors and 221 conditions (15 categories) for the hierarchical factor (OR=0.75-1.94). Circulatory, digestive, and respiratory diseases were linked to neurodevelopmental, internalizing, and substance use liabilities. Metabolic conditions were negatively associated with thought and compulsive liabilities but positively associated with the remaining three factors. Laboratory results, particularly lipid and glucose metabolism markers, supported these differential findings. Immune markers also showed differential associations, with C-reactive protein and Complement C4 specifically linked to neurodevelopmental and thought factors, respectively. Similar trends emerged in the smaller African-like ancestry sample. Interpretation Overall, these findings support ongoing efforts to define biologically informed subtypes in psychiatry, such as immuno-metabolic profiles, which can facilitate patient stratification in clinical trials and support transdiagnostic precision psychiatry approaches. Funding The work was supported by funding from the participating institutions. BF's and NRM's contributions were supported by the European Community's Horizon 2020 Programme (H2020/2014-2020) under grant agreement No. 847879 (PRIME). NRM was also supported by the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research (NWO) Innovation Programme (Vidi grant No. 09150172410043). Research reported in this publication was also supported by the National Institute of Mental Health of the National Institutes of Health under Award Number R01MH124851. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the funders.

papers.title: Genome-Wide Study of Early Disability Severity in Multiple Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by demyelination and neuroaxonal injury. MS genetic susceptibility and severity long after disease onset is well characterized, but the genetic architecture of disability severity near disease onset is unclear. We performed the first genome-wide association study of early MS severity to identify causal loci, prioritize effector genes and associated pathways, and understand the relationships of early MS severity and various traits. Methods: The primary outcome was the first age-related MS severity score (ARMSS), an age-adjusted severity measure, in 7,209 individuals of Swedish discovery cohorts and independent Italian and multi-national European replication cohorts. Replicated loci underwent conditional analysis, fine-mapping, time-to-event MS phenotype association analyses, and multi-omics-based gene prioritization. Using the genome-wide summary statistics, we also conducted heritability analyses, polygenic risk score association with other MS phenotypes, gene-level and pathway analyses, cross-trait analyses with disease-related traits, Mendelian randomization, and drug-repurposing screening. Results: Two suggestive loci were replicated: rs1234317 at chromosome 1 (effect allele T: beta = 0.100, SE = 0.0189, P = 1.08E-07) and rs929769 at chromosome 5 (effect allele T: beta = -0.0956, SE = 0.0184, P = 1.95E-07). Fine-mapping supported rs929769 as a single-variant 95% credible set, and rs1234317 and rs6657136 as a two-variant 95% credible set with two-causal-SNP model having the highest posterior probability. The SNPs did not show a significant change in effect sizes when adjusted for heritable traits and exhibited attenuated associations with long-term MS disability progression. TNFSF4 was the top prioritized effector for rs1234317, TNFSF18 for rs6657136, and ADAMTS2 for rs929769. Early MS severity showed partial genetic overlap with MS susceptibility or late MS severity, but no significant correlation with a range of neurological, psychiatric, autoimmune, cognitive, and aging traits. Pathway analyses identified ion-channel regulation and folic acid metabolism, and Mendelian randomization suggested nominal bidirectional associations with educational attainment. Drug screening nominated several drugs that can be repurposed. Discussion: This study identifies candidate causal variants of early MS severity and their effector genes: TNFSF4, TNFSF18, and ADAMTS2. It provides insights into the genetic architecture and therapeutic measures for the early phase of MS severity.

papers.title: Pooled Multiplex Amplicon Massive Parallel Sequencing for High-Throughput Confirmation of Whole-Genome Sequencing Potentially Pathogenic Variants in Patients with Parkinsonism
papers.abstract: Whole-genome sequencing identifies large numbers of genetic variants, although only a subset requires independent confirmation for clinical interpretation. Sanger sequencing remains the standard confirmation method but is impractical for large-scale variant verification. We developed and evaluated a strategy for variant confirmation based on multi-amplicon massively parallel sequencing of pooled DNA samples. Whole-genome sequencing data were obtained from 86 individuals, including patients with parkinsonism and controls. Variants were selected using phenotype-driven filtering, ClinVar classification, and pathogenicity assessment criteria. A total of 307 variants were targeted using a custom amplicon panel comprising 290 amplicons. DNA samples were normalized, pooled into 16 mixtures, and sequenced following automated library preparation. Variant presence and sequencing quality were assessed using standard bioinformatic tools. Of the 307 selected variants, 243 were successfully confirmed. Unconfirmed variants included sequencing artifacts (18), insufficiently covered targets (5), large insertions or deletions exceeding 12 base pairs (36), and variants located within homopolymeric regions (5). Results for selected variants were concordant with Sanger sequencing, and observed variant frequencies corresponded to expected frequencies in pooled samples. This approach provides a robust, rapid, and cost-effective method for high-throughput genetic variants confirming identified by whole-genome sequencing while requiring only limited DNA input. Despite complete concordance with Sanger sequencing, larger validation studies are needed before multi-amplicon massively parallel sequencing can replace routine confirmatory testing.

papers.title: Assessing the Accuracy of the NeuroBooster Array for GBA1 Variant Detection
papers.abstract: GBA1 variants are major Parkinson's disease risk factors, but their detection is challenging. We compared NeuroBooster Array (NBA) genotyping with reference sequencing in 3,744 individuals. NBA correctly identified 520/608 carriers (85.5%). Of 89 missed calls, 73 had no matching probe and 16 had missing calls. 25 participants had false positive calls. NBA should not be used alone for clinical decisions, but is very useful for case control analysis.

papers.title: Inactivating mutations in polyadenylation factor CSTF2 disrupt intronic polyadenylation patterns and are associated with intellectual disability.
papers.abstract: Alternative polyadenylation contributes extensively to transcript diversification and is particularly prominent during neuronal differentiation. CSTF2 encodes an RNA-binding subunit of the cleavage stimulation factor complex and has previously been associated with X-linked intellectual disability through a single Asp50Ala missense variant with increased RNA-binding activity. Here, we identify seven rare CSTF2 variants in ten hemizygous male probands with intellectual disability, global developmental delay and/or autism spectrum disorder, including missense, nonsense, splice-site, and frameshift variants. We functionally assessed selected variants by ectopic expression in CSTF2-depleted HEK293T cells, followed by total and 3'-end-proximal RNA sequencing. Phe19Leu, Gln543Ter and Leu555Ser markedly impaired CSTF2 function. These variants predominantly reduced the usage of strong, evolutionarily conserved intronic polyadenylation sites with prominent GU-rich sequences, while increasing the usage of downstream sites within terminal 3'UTRs. In contrast, the previously reported Asp50Ala variant produced an opposing pattern, with preferential activation of intronic polyadenylation sites, consistent with its increased RNA-binding activity. These findings data provide genetic and functional support for CSTF2 as an X-linked intellectual disability, identify inactivating CSTF2 variants as a disease mechanism, and imply that both reduced and increased CSTF2 activity can result in neurodevelopmental disorder.

papers.title: Excluded causal variants produce false discoveries in genetic fine-mapping
papers.abstract: Statistical fine-mapping seeks to distinguish causal genetic variants from correlated variants in linkage disequilibrium (LD). Although fine-mapping algorithms perform well in simulations, they are often applied in settings that violate their assumptions. In particular, genome-wide association study (GWAS) and quantitative trait locus (QTL) workflows routinely omit variants with minor allele frequency (MAf) below 1% and most insertions and deletions (indels), excluding many causal variants before fine-mapping begins. To assess this empirically, we compared filtered and unfiltered fine-mapping at 499 All of Us loci. Twenty percent of high-confidence calls after a 1% MAf filter, and 32% when indels were also omitted, lacked support in the unfiltered analysis. Errors were particularly enriched when tested variants tagged an omitted variant, so fine-mapping misassigned its signal to a proxy variant. At RBO, omitting the frameshift that defines blood group O gave near-certain posterior inclusion probabilities (PIPs) to linked single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). To address this disconnect, we developed SuSiE-OUT, which enables fine-mapping in scenarios with possibly omitted causal variants. Modeling infinitesimal effects did not reliably prevent these errors, whereas imputing omitted variants or modeling them with our SuSiE-OUT method prevented most errors. Overall, we find that common analysis workflows substantially increase false discoveries in fine-mapping analyses, and we demonstrate two approaches to mitigate this challenge.

papers.title: Genetic effects on serum and urine metabolites across ancestries and their links to disease
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies of the metabolome have predominantly examined European-ancestry populations using a single biofluid, constraining both the discovery of metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs) and the resolution of causal variant finemapping. Here, we report a multi-ancestry genome-wide association study of 1,955 serum and urine metabolites in 4,431 European American and African American participants from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study. We identify 969 mQTLs for 553 metabolites, 30% unreported in studies of matched biofluid and ancestry, and replicate 91-99% of testable mQTLs in two independent cohorts. In the African American sample with balanced sample sizes, 36% of metabolites with mQTLs are serum-specific, 39% urine-specific, and 25% shared, demonstrating complementary genetic architecture. Only 23 of 632 candidate ancestry-specific mQTLs show heterogeneous effects beyond variant availability and power, yet allele frequency differences expose functional variants such as an SLC28A1 splice variant, virtually absent in Europeans, that increases urine uridine excretion, implicating impaired CNT1-mediated renal nucleoside reabsorption. Multi-ancestry finemapping improves credible set resolution, and colocalization with the Million Veteran Program phenome links the catalog to cardiometabolic, kidney and liver traits consistent with prioritized gene function. Integrating biofluids and ancestries enhances genetic discovery and mechanistic characterization of the human metabolome.

papers.title: Improving Consistency in Colorectal Cancer Genetic Risk Assessment and Return of Results Through an Integrated Polygenic Risk Score
papers.abstract: BackgroundPublished colorectal cancer (CRC) polygenic risk scores (PRS) may demonstrate similar population-level predictive performance but often assign substantially different risk classifications to the same individuals. Such discordance presents challenges for clinical implementation and return of results (RoR). MethodsWe developed a stable PRS for CRC (stPRS-CRC) by integrating 28 published PRS using PRSmix in the All of Us (AoU) development cohort (n=321,703). Performance was evaluated in a held-out AoU validation cohort (n=80,423) and independently validated in the Genomic Health Initiative (GHI) (n=17,545). CRC associations were assessed using logistic regression, comparing individuals in the highest PRS decile with the remaining 90%. Individual-level concordance in high-risk classification was evaluated using mean Jaccard indices. ResultsPublished CRC PRS showed substantial discordance in individual-level high-risk classification despite generally consistent associations with CRC. stPRS-CRC integrated information from multiple published PRS and demonstrated CRC associations comparable to PGS003852, the strongest-performing individual PRS. The odds ratios for stPRS-CRC were 1.94 (95% CI, 1.79-2.11) in AoU development, 2.08 (1.76-2.45) in AoU validation, and 2.08 (1.55-2.79) in GHI. Mean Jaccard indices using stPRS-CRC versus PGS003852 as anchors, each compared with the same 27 published PRS, were 0.29 versus 0.20, 0.43 versus 0.25, and 0.27 versus 0.19, respectively (all P<0.001). ConclusionsIntegrating multiple published CRC PRS significantly improved individual-level concordance in high-risk classification while maintaining population-level predictive performance. stPRS-CRC may provide a more consistent framework for clinical genetic risk assessment and ROR.

papers.title: A novel patient with inherited TNF deficiency and tuberculosis
papers.abstract: Two otherwise healthy patients from Colombia, now aged 30 and 38 years, developed pulmonary tuberculosis due to inherited, complete TNF deficiency at the ages of 19 and 18 years. We report here a previously healthy Iranian patient with inherited complete TNF deficiency who was diagnosed with both pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB between 10 and 15 years of age. The homozygous TNF variant (c.673C>T) introduces a premature stop codon (TNF p.Q225*) resulting in losses of expression and function. Despite normal myeloid and lymphoid subset development, the patients primary leukocytes do not secrete detectable amounts of TNF. As in the TNF-deficient Colombian patients, the respiratory burst of GM-CSF-derived macrophages is impaired. Our findings expand the spectrum of TB phenotypes in patients with TNF deficiency and confirm that TNF is essential for immunity to M. tuberculosis in humans but apparently redundant against many other pathogens, including weakly virulent mycobacteria.

papers.title: Functional analysis enables reclassification of SCN1A missense variants of uncertain significance in epilepsy
papers.abstract: SCN1A, the most prominent gene for epilepsy, encodes the pore-forming subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel, NaV1.1. Loss-of-function variants reduce NaV1.1 activity in inhibitory neurons leading to hyperexcitability; they are associated with a spectrum of epilepsies, from self-limited phenotypes in genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus, to the prototypic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, Dravet syndrome. Thousands of SCN1A missense variants have been identified, but determining pathogenicity using ACMG criteria can be challenging. Currently, 48% of missense SCN1A variants in ClinVar are classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS). We aimed to provide functional evidence to inform variant classification using a high-throughput automated patch-clamp assay. We validated our assay using 27 true pathogenic SCN1A variants and 25 true benign variants. The results show that 17/27 true pathogenic variants from patients with Dravet syndrome showed severe reductions in current density, precluding gating analysis. Of the remaining ten true pathogenic variants, seven showed an increased voltage difference between the midpoints of activation and inactivation (V0.5diff). Current density and V0.5diff were combined within a graded Bayesian framework to derive a functional log-likelihood ratio reflecting the magnitude of loss of function. We then applied our validated assay to 16 SCN1A missense variants detected in an Australian cohort: three likely pathogenic, one likely benign and 12 VUSs. These variants occurred in 31 individuals from 16 families with a broad phenotypic spectrum, including four individuals with Dravet syndrome who carried p.Ser243Phe, p.Met973Val or p.Lys1911Glu. All three variants showed loss of function: p.Ser243Phe had reduced current density, whereas p.Met973Val and p.Lys1911Glu had abnormal V0.5diff despite current density within the normal range. Of these 16 variants, ten have combined functional scores consistent with abnormal functional evidence. Combining our functional evidence with ACMG criteria, our findings changed the classification of eight of 16 variants (50%), with six of 12 VUS reclassified as likely pathogenic and two of three likely pathogenic variants upgraded to pathogenic. We show that calibrated automated patch-clamp assays can provide actionable functional data to enable the interpretation and reclassification of SCN1A variants and inform clinical care, allowing therapeutic optimisation and facilitating access to genetic therapies.

papers.title: Polygenic Prediction of Depression Liability Reveals Broad Genetic Associations Across Development, Families, and Populations
papers.abstract: Polygenic prediction of depression is limited by the depth of depression phenotyping available at biobank scale as well as sample size. Here we develop a depression score combining information from depression and genetically correlated psychiatric traits using phenotype reconstruction, multi-trait genetic integration and Bayesian effect estimation. Compared with the strongest publicly available depression-only score (Psychiatric Genomics Consortium 2025, excluding 23andMe), the liability-R2 for depression in UK Biobank rose by 49.7% and within-family standardized associations with latent internalizing were up to 54% larger. Across 2,328 childhood and adolescent outcomes in the ABCD study, the association profile of the integrated score was almost identical to that of the depression-only score (r = 0.99), while being uniformly stronger. 1,494 outcomes related to mood, behavior, social functioning, hobbies and sleep were associated with the score -- 423 of them within-family. In ABCD, adolescents in the highest score decile were 3.5 times as likely as those in the lowest decile to report suicidal thoughts by age 14 (23% versus 7%) and 1.9 times as likely to report nicotine or cannabis use by age 17 (47% versus 25%). In adults, the score predicted worse general health, chronic pain, and life dissatisfaction. Associations with psychiatric symptoms were substantially stronger in girls than in boys (boys coeffiicients 0.68 times girls), particularly for girl-typical symptoms, and showed no moderation by household resources, hardship or deprivation that remained significant after correction for multiple testing. Prediction was attenuated in line with genetic distance from training data for Hispanic and African American children. Depression prediction can thus be strengthened substantially by integrating the internalizing spectrum, without detectable loss of specificity or within-family predictive ability.

papers.title: Pathogenic MYRF ICA Domain Variant is Aberrantly Trafficked in the RPE and Results in Isolated Nanophthalmos
papers.abstract: PurposeMyelin regulatory factor is a transcription factor essential for RPE development and serves as a critical "GO" signal for eye growth. Pathogenic variants in MYRF manifest in a spectrum of clinical phenotypes ranging from isolated nanophthalmos to severe syndromic disease, in a gene dosage dependent manner. In this study, we aimed to determine the pathogenicity and molecular mechanism of a novel variant in the MYRF ICA domain, c.2083C>T (p.R695C), that leads to isolated nanophthalmos and mild retinal pigment epithelial disruption. MethodsWhole genome sequencing was performed and identified a novel MYRF variant. Pathogenecity and in silico modeling were evaluated using the Ensembl VEP tool and PyMOL. Human primary RPE and/or ARPE-19 cells were transduced with FLAG-tagged variant and wildtype MYRF or double-tagged FLAG-MYRF-MYC proteins to evaluate transcriptional activity, localization, and protein trafficking. ResultsIn silico modeling supports variant pathogenicity and altered homotrimer conformation. Functional studies in human primary RPE (hRPE) and/or ARPE-19 cells confirmed that MYRF p.R695C is cleavage deficient, mislocalized to the apical surface of polarized RPE, and demonstrated reduced synergistic transcriptional activity with co-factor SOX10 in HEK293T cells. Protein trafficking studies demonstrated that wildtype MYRF is trafficked to the apical cell surface and plasma membrane and that endogenous MYRF requires ER to Golgi trafficking pathways for proper nuclear localization and cleavage dynamics. ConclusionsTogether, these results confirm that p.R695C is pathogenic for nanophthalmos, implicate trafficking as a regulatory mechanism of MYRF in the hRPE, and support that RPE disruption as a feature of MYRF-associated nanophthalmos.

papers.title: A Framework for Variant Filtering to Improve Diagnostic Outcomes in Genome Sequencing
papers.abstract: Rare genetic disorders frequently remain undiagnosed despite the use of exome sequencing (ES) and genome sequencing (GS). This study aimed to enhance diagnostic yield by introducing a systematic framework: SMART filtering (Systematic, Multi-step, Automated, Rare variant prioritization Tool), designed to optimize GS analysis, with a particular emphasis on non-coding regions. We retrospectively analyzed 153 cases with previously negative ES and GS results. SMART filtering was applied as a pre-annotation filtering step, integrating conservation metrics, allele frequency thresholds, and splicing prediction scores. Then followed by phenotype-based prioritization and manual review. Application of this framework identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 4.6% of cases, strong variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in 1.3%, and additional candidate variants in 5.2% of cases. Several deep-intronic variants were confirmed by RNA studies and segregation analyses. The framework enabled efficient prioritization of non-coding and regulatory variants that were overlooked by standard analyses. In conclusion, SMART filtering offers a reproducible and scalable strategy to improve diagnostic yield in GS, particularly in cases where conventional analysis methods fall short. Integrating such frameworks into clinical genomic pipelines can enhance variant interpretability and diagnostic performance, ultimately leading to better patient care outcomes.

papers.title: Investigating the potential effect of topiramate on anorexia nervosa and binge eating behaviour using drug-target Mendelian randomization
papers.abstract: Topiramate is an antiseizure medication used to treat epilepsy and migraine and is commonly prescribed for appetite suppression and weight loss. However, whether its pharmacological actions influence eating disorder risk remains unclear. We applied drug-target Mendelian randomization (MR) to investigate potential causal effects of topiramate on the risk of anorexia nervosa (AN; 24,223 cases and 1,243,971 controls) and binge-eating behaviour (BE; 39,279 cases and 1,227,436 controls) and, exploratorily, eight other psychiatric disorders: attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety disorders, alcohol use disorder, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and schizophrenia. We used summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) to investigate genetically predicted pharmacological actions of topiramate using brain- and blood-derived cis-expression quantitative trait loci for genes encoding its molecular targets. Five genetic instruments consistent with topiramates antiepileptic action were validated: CA4 and CACNB3 expression in the brain and CA4, GRIK1, and GRIK3 expression in the blood. Robustness of the findings was assessed using SMR-multi, HEIDI, and colocalization analyses. After multiple-testing correction, genetically predicted inhibition of CA4 expression in blood was associated with decreased BE risk (OR = 0.867, 95% CI = 0.792-0.950, p = 0.002) and remained significant in SMR-multi (p = 0.0049). Colocalization provided moderate support for a shared causal variant underlying CA4 expression and BE (PPH4 = 0.58). No robust evidence was identified for AN or the eight exploratory psychiatric outcomes. Overall, our findings warrant further clinical and functional investigations into mechanisms underlying topiramate-associated appetite suppression and weight loss and their relevance to eating-disorder risk.

papers.title: Shared additive- and variance-associated genetic architecture of cardiac structure and function
papers.abstract: Cardiac remodeling underlies cardiomyopathy and heart failure, yet how common genetic effects are organized across the four chambers, and whether they influence phenotypic variability beyond additive genetic effects, remains unclear. We analyzed 22 cardiac magnetic resonance phenotypes in up to 77,271 UK Biobank participants. Additive mapping identified 748 locus-trait associations across 239 regions. Multivariate fine-mapping revealed that 96% of signals showed effects across multiple cardiac chambers, while resolving independent signals with distinct anatomical profiles, including predominantly atrial and ventricular signals at RBM20. Fine-mapped signal sharing formed three robust communities corresponding broadly to atrial function, chamber remodeling and ventricular systolic function. Variance mapping identified 19 associations, 13 without a nearby additive signal. Individual variance loci and polygenic effects generalized to clinical echocardiographic phenotypes and outcomes in the Penn Medicine Biobank. These findings reveal cardiac common-variant architecture as broadly shared yet locally heterogeneous and identify phenotypic variability as a partly distinct genetic dimension.

papers.title: Single-Cell Transcriptome-Wide Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization Analysis Reveals Immune Cell-Specific Mechanisms in Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo integrate single-cell expression quantitative trait locus (sc-eQTL), Alzheimers disease (AD) genome-wide association study (GWAS), and Bayesian colocalization analyses, in order to systematically identify candidate causal genes and potential immune mechanisms that specifically regulate AD risk in peripheral immune cells. MethodsUsing the cis-eQTLs of 14 peripheral blood immune cell types from the OneK1K single-cell eQTL dataset as exposure data and the AD GWAS (GCST90565439) as outcome data, a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis was performed. Weak instrumental variables were removed using F-statistics, and approximately independent genetic instruments were obtained by linkage disequilibrium pruning. For significant gene-cell type associations, compareCluster functional enrichment, Bayesian colocalization, and phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) were further performed, and the 1M-scBloodNL dataset was used for replication validation. ResultsThe MR analysis identified 187 gene-cell type associations significantly associated with AD risk, involving 161 candidate causal genes. Among them, 141 genes showed significant associations in only a single immune cell type, suggesting that AD-related immune genetic regulation has marked cell type specificity. Functional enrichment analysis showed that the significant genes in different immune cell types were enriched in biological processes including MHC class II antigen presentation, phagocytosis, membrane invagination, and positive regulation of T cell activation. Colocalization analysis indicated a strong shared genetic signal between TNF expression in CD4+SOX4+ T cells and AD risk (PP.H4 = 0.833). In the 1M-scBloodNL replication analysis, several candidate genes showed consistent direction and nominal significance. The PheWAS results suggested that the significant phenotypic associations of the TNF instrumental variable were mainly concentrated in immune- and hematology-related traits, with no genome-wide significant neurological phenotypic associations observed. ConclusionThis study suggests that single-cell eQTL-MR combined with colocalization analysis can be used to dissect the cell type-specific genetic regulatory mechanisms of peripheral immunity in AD. The genetically predicted expression of TNF in CD4+SOX4+ T cells may represent an important immune-related signal for AD risk, but further validation in independent populations and functional experiments is still required.

papers.title: A multi-center retrospective chart analysis identifying clinical, biochemical, and radiographic signatures of short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1) deficiency
papers.abstract: Short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1) catalyzes the hydration of C4-C6 acyl-CoA molecules to produce ATP in fatty acid {beta}-oxidation. Deficiency of the ECHS1 enzyme, ECHS1D, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that presents with a large and pleomorphic clinical spectrum. We present the largest comprehensive study of known diagnosed ECHS1D patients to date, reporting 26 new patients and 8 novel variants in conjunction with a literature review of 87 previously reported patients. All patients were categorized into neonatal, infantile, and late-onset groups based on age of onset and clinical course. Neonatal-onset cases were characterized by early and severe multisystem disease, often with lactic acidosis, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, and high early mortality (62.5%). The infantile-onset group was heterogeneous, but many exhibited hallmark features such as dystonia, developmental delay, and basal ganglia involvement on neuroimaging. Mortality was significantly lower than the neonatal cohort (24.4%). Late-onset patients had more localized neurologic symptoms, particularly dystonia, and significantly lower mortality overall (0%). Moreover, we report a 37.5% survival rate in newly reported neonatal onset patients compared with 18.2% in prior reports, possibly reflective of earlier recognition of ECHS1D and greater utilization of therapies including N-acetylcysteine, sodium dichloroacetate, and valine-restricted diet.

papers.title: Evolution-guided association mapping using long-read genomes from a self-identified Black or African American cohort in All of Us
papers.abstract: BackgroundIdentifying functional variants that influence human health remains a challenge in human genetics. Conventional genotype-phenotype association studies test millions of variants, imposing a substantial multiple-testing burden as genomic and biobank datasets expand in size and variant diversity. Additionally, the contribution of structural variation, which is a substantial driver of genetic diversity, remains underexplored in these studies. Signatures of recent positive selection offer a powerful biological basis for prioritizing potentially functional variation, although demographic history can confound their detection and interpretation in these analyses. ResultsWe performed evolution-guided association mapping using long-read genomes from 1,027 self-identified Black or African American participants in the All of Us Research Program and short-read genomes from an additional 38,552 matched participants of African-ancestry. Using demography-calibrated inferences, we identified 228 genomic regions with local ancestry enrichment or depletion and 1,616 candidate loci showing putative recent positive selection signals. These loci were enriched for genic and regulatory sequences, as well as previously reported eQTL, sQTL, and GWAS associations. Leveraging the resolution of the long-read data, we mapped 15 structural variants to these candidate loci, including 10 located within 1,000 base pairs of putative cis-regulatory enhancers. Admixture- and selection-based phenome-wide association testing identified 13 and 446 nominal associations, respectively, 17 of which remained significant following replication and meta-analysis. ConclusionsOur results support the use of evolutionary signatures as a robust framework for uncovering clinically relevant variation, including structural variants, in underrepresented populations.

papers.title: A Global Atlas of Immune Alleles Reveals Health-Relevant Variation Across Groups
papers.abstract: Immune allele frequencies inform disease association mapping, pharmacogenomic guidance, and vaccine design, yet such data are missing for most of the worlds groups. Here we present the Global Atlas of Immune Alleles (GAIA), applying benchmarked genotyping tools across the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA), Immunoglobulin Heavy Chain Constant (IGHC), and Fc Gamma Receptor (FCGR) loci to whole-genome sequencing data from 20,248 individuals, oversampling sub-Saharan African, Island Southeast Asian, and Pacific groups. Despite representing fewer than 0.5% of observations in the Allele Frequency Net Database, GAIA expands the databases catalogue by 38%, demonstrating that representation matters more than sample size. We identify HLA alleles at group-specific frequencies that challenge pharmacogenomic screening recommendations and document disease-risk alleles common in groups lacking clinical guidance. Finally, we introduce majority allelic diversity (MAD-X), which counts the alleles required for X% of individuals in a group to carry at least one, and show that reaching 90% HLA-B coverage for vaccine design requires up to 2.7 times more alleles in underrepresented groups than in those of Northwest European ancestry.

papers.title: A population-based resource for the prioritization of rare variants of unknown significance in clinical genomics
papers.abstract: Rare diseases represent a major public health challenge because they are often associated with severe phenotypes, yet many causal variants remain undiscovered. Founder populations provide a unique opportunity to identify disease-causing variants through the local enrichment of rare alleles. Using whole-genome sequencing data from individuals in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean population, enriched variants were identified and their founder status was assessed through identity-by-descent sharing. Variant impact was evaluated using functional prediction tools without relying on prior clinical classification. A total of 131 founder variants of interest were identified, most of which would likely have been overlooked by conventional approaches based on existing clinical annotations. We developed a web-based platform that facilitates clinician access to the latest interpretation of their genetic variants of interest. These findings demonstrate that potentially pathogenic variants can remain undetected even in extensively studied founder populations. More broadly, they highlight the value of population structure-based approaches for uncovering rare disease variants and improving the characterization of genetic disease risk across human populations.

papers.title: Unravelling the mechanisms of clozapine-induced neutropenia in treatment-resistant schizophrenia using cellular genomics
papers.abstract: Background: About one-third of individuals with schizophrenia do not respond to first-line antipsychotics. Clozapine has superior efficacy for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), yet remains underutilised partly due to a 1% risk of potentially fatal clozapine-induced neutropenia (CIN). However, the biological mechanisms underlying CIN remain poorly understood. Methods: We recruited six individuals with TRS who had previously received clozapine: three who ceased clozapine following CIN and three who stopped for reasons unrelated to CIN. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were collected and cultured in vitro under three conditions: untreated, clozapine alone, or clozapine with its two major metabolites. Single nucleus RNA sequencing was performed to profile the cellular transcriptomic landscape following exposure to clozapine and its metabolites. Results: After quality control, 59,313 cells spanning 26 distinct clusters were retained. Multiple cell type-specific genes were differentially expressed in TRS with CIN, or in response to clozapine exposure in TRS donors with CIN (but not in those without CIN), after adjusting for age, sex and smoking status. We also identified a CIN-associated co-expression module in naive CD4 T cells that was driven by the transcription factor SREBF1, and robust evidence for differential cell-cell communication involving seven intercellular ligand-receptor pairs. There was limited evidence that clozapine-related metabolites contributed to these transcriptional changes. Conclusions: Our findings provide novel insights into cell type-specific transcriptional changes associated with CIN status and/or clozapine exposure in TRS with CIN. With replication in larger, independent cohorts, this work may contribute to the future development of predictive biomarkers for CIN and safer therapeutic strategies for TRS.

papers.title: Variant Classification of a Non-Protein Coding Gene: ACMG/AMP Specifications for RMRP from the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel
papers.abstract: PurposeThis study, conducted by the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel (ClinGen SCID-VCEP), aimed to adapt the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) framework for germline variant interpretation in RMRP. Unlike the protein-coding genes for which the framework was primarily developed, RMRP encodes a non-protein-coding RNA. Biallelic pathogenic variants in RMRP cause cartilage-hair hypoplasia, which can include severe combined immunodeficiency disease and other immune abnormalities. MethodsAn RMRP-focused SCID-VCEP subgroup reviewed all 28 ACMG/AMP evidence criteria using population databases, published clinical and experimental data, computational predictions, and expert consensus. Each criterion was retained, modified, or designated as not applicable based on RMRP biology and disease mechanisms. The resulting specifications were pilot tested using 27 variants selected from ClinVar and research laboratory data. ResultsFifteen ACMG/AMP criteria were determined to be applicable to RMRP, while 13 were considered not applicable. Several criteria were modified to evaluate nucleotide-level effects on transcriptional regulation, critical promoter regions, and RNA secondary structure. The specifications also incorporated RMRP-specific recommendations for population frequency, functional evidence, variant phase, segregation, and phenotype. Application of the specifications classified 6 variants as pathogenic, 10 as likely pathogenic, 7 as variants of uncertain significance, and 4 as benign. Previously pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants remained within the pathogenic spectrum, and all previously benign variants remained benign. Variants with conflicting ClinVar interpretations were resolved as either likely pathogenic or uncertain. PM1, PM3, and PP4 were the primary criteria supporting pathogenic classifications. ConclusionThe SCID-VCEP specifications provide a standardized approach to the classification of germline RMRP variants in cartilage-hair hypoplasia and demonstrate how the ACMG/AMP framework can be adapted for a disease-associated non-protein-coding RNA gene. These specifications support the development of variant interpretation frameworks for other clinically relevant non-protein-coding genes.
